name: Southern Pomo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Walker, Neil Alexander. 2013. A Grammar of Southern Pomo: An Indigenous Language of California. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara. (PDF via Internet Archive copy of wieldoc.org; quotes Halpern 1984: 38.)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.2.3 Stress, pp. 72-74; sec. 2.6 (clitic tests), pp. 92-93; p. 134 (vowel deletion and weight)
catalog_quote: Stress in Southern Pomo is predictable: primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a phrase. ... Halpern confirms this for Southern Pomo and elaborates on the basic stress patterns in the language: The general rule, subject to some optionality, for non-phonemic accent in [Southern Pomo] is that loudest stress accompanied by raised pitch, both with falling contour, occurs on the penult of a breath-group, with secondary stress normally falling on every second syllable preceding the penult. (Halpern 1984: 38) ... [p.92] Southern Pomo stress, as described earlier in §2.2.3, is completely regular: the penultimate syllable bears primary stress with every other syllable bearing secondary stress to the left of the penult. However, a matter not touched upon in §2.2.3 is the unit of which the stressed syllable is the penult. ... The assignment of stress in Southern Pomo, therefore, is no…

audit.reasoning: The classification (phrasal/breath-group penultimate primary stress, alternating secondary leftward, weight-blind, post-clitic) rests on the standard modern reference grammar (Walker 2013, 680 pp), which we hold and whose deciding passages are verbatim at the cited pages (72-73, 92-93, 134). Glottolog's only other descriptive work is the 2020 published edition of the same grammar. The underlying primary statement (Halpern 1984:38) is quoted in full inside the held source, and the one instrumental study (Walker 2008 MA) is by the same author and summarized with its data in the held grammar. Nothing seen suggests the classification would change; works still to obtain are confirmatory only.org returned a WAF challenge, so was created but is empty.

sources.citation: Kaplan, Max J. 2020. Southern Pomo syncope is metrically conditioned: metrical opacity and stratal derivation. Proceedings of the Linguistic Society of America 5(1): 584-598 [article 4736]. doi:10.3765/plsa.v5i1.4736.

tone.quote: Main stress in Southern Pomo falls on the penult (in words in isolation), with iterating secondary stresses on every other syllable from right to left (McLendon 1973; Walker 2020). That is, the surface metrical structure counts from the right edge of the word in what has been characterised as a trochaic system (Buckley 2019), though I assume an unbracketed grid-based approach (Prince 1983). Stress is quantity-insensitive: it falls on both light and heavy syllables, is not attracted to heavy syllables and is strictly alternating. ... surface stress in both Southern Pomo and Kashaya is assigned in a domain larger than the word, described as the 'phrase' (Buckley 2019; Walker 2020: 49) or 'breath-group' (Halpern 1984: 38).
tone.locator: sec. 2.2.2 'Syncope, stress and metrical structure', p. 607; sec. 2.2.3 'Syncope as a phrasal phenomenon', p. 608 (fn. 13 on trisyllabic nouns, p. 607)
tone.summary: No tone statement; prosody described purely as quantity-insensitive penultimate stress with alternating secondary stress, computed over the phrase.

sources.citation: Buckley, Eugene. 2019. Change and contact in Pomoan stress patterns. Talk presented to the Group in American Indian Languages (GAIL), University of California, Berkeley, 2 May 2019. Slides (78 pp.),https://www.ling.upenn.edu/~gene/papers/Buckley2019_pomoan_stress_GAIL.pdf.

tone.quote: Modern stress: Southern Pomo • regular penultimate stress – reported to be on the phrase, not just the word • outlier in Pomoan – right-orientation – all others are left-oriented (but NE?) • secondary stress – on alternating syllables preceding the penult ... Southern Pomo analysis • quantity-insensitive trochees, primary stress at right (σNσ) (σNσ) (σPσ) – iterative from right to left, a very common pattern • can be constructed across phrases – shares this property with Kashaya • antepenult in trisyllables is stressed, and typically heavy
tone.locator: slides 41 'Modern stress: Southern Pomo' and 44 'Southern Pomo analysis' (also 42-43 data, 61-64 Miwok contact reanalysis)
tone.summary: No tone or pitch accent claimed for Southern Pomo; pitch accent is a property of Northern Pomo and Kashaya in this survey; Southern Pomo = penultimate phrasal stress.

sources.note: Secondary basis only: Kaplan 2023 (p. 607) cites 'McLendon 1973; Walker 2020' as the sources for Southern Pomo penultimate main stress with right-to-left secondary stresses, and Walker 2013 lists it among his phonological sources; so it carries a per-language stress statement for Southern Pomo within a Proto-Pomo stress reconstruction. Whether it comments on pitch/tone for Southern Pomo is unknown.
